The lives and contributions of these exemplars inspire and guide us in the preservation, renewal and civilisational rebuilding of Sanatana Bharat, while instilling in us a deeper sense of duty towards it. These ten are but a few among the many who shaped, defended and enriched our civilisation. Their selection is illustrative, not exhaustive; it honours these exemplars without diminishing the greatness of those who are not listed.

Maharshi Veda Vyasa’s fundamental contribution was to give Hindu civilisation an intellectual, scriptural and civilisational architecture capable of integrating its vast and diverse sacred inheritance. Through the systematisation of the Vedas, the Mahabharata and the Bhagavad Gita, he brought together its fundamental teachings on dharma, karma, jnana, bhakti and moksha into a coherent framework that could be understood and transmitted across generations. The Puranas further carried this inheritance into households, temples and regional communities through narrative, cosmology, genealogy and devotion. In essence, Vyasa gave Hindu civilisation its mind—its metaphysical foundations, scriptural coherence and civilisational memory, together with the intellectual vocabulary through which its inheritance could be understood and transmitted.
Maharshi Veda Vyasa stands as the First Architect of Hindu Civilisation.

Adi Sankaracharya’s fundamental contribution was to build the institutional armature necessary to preserve and transmit Vyasa’s intellectual inheritance. Through Advaita Vedanta, the Mathas and the Dasanami order, he restored philosophical, monastic and pedagogical coherence to a fragmented Hindu society. By integrating śāstra (scriptural authority) with śastra (disciplined force) and establishing enduring networks of monastic and religious authority, he strengthened Hindu civilisation’s capacity to withstand political disruption and iconoclastic destruction. In essence, Adi Sankaracharya gave Hindu civilisation its organisational body—the institutional authority, disciplined order and civilisational resilience required to carry Vyasa’s inheritance through centuries of upheaval.
Adi Sankaracharya stands as the Second Architect of Hindu Civilisation.

Swami Karpatri Maharaj’s historic contribution was to carry the cause of Sanatana Dharma into the political life of independent India. Through the Rama Rajya Parishad, his writings, and his leadership of the Goraksha movement, he challenged the emerging political order to respect Dharma, protect Hindu religious institutions and preserve the civilisational foundations of Hindu society. He gave organised political expression to the conviction that India’s freedom must serve, not sever, its Sanatana civilisational inheritance.

Raja Manu Neethi Cholan (2nd century BCE), associated with Urayur in present-day Tamil Nadu, stands as an enduring embodiment of Hindu Dharma, justice and the king’s sacred duty to protect the cow. His original name was Raja Ellalan, while he became renowned by the title “Manu Neethi Cholan,” signifying a king who upheld Manu’s principles of righteous justice. Outside his palace hung the Dharma Ghanta—the Bell of Justice—which anyone could ring to seek the king’s intervention. When the chariot of his son killed a calf, the grieving cow is said to have pulled the bell with its horn, seeking justice. Placing Dharma above paternal love, the king ordered the execution of his son so that, as a father, he too would endure the same agony of putra-viyoga—the loss of a son—that the cow had suffered. His story embodies the profound Hindu ideal that Dharma stands above blood, power and privilege, and that the ruler must protect even the voiceless. Fittingly, his statue adorns the Madras High Court premises as a symbol of uncompromising justice.

Maharaja Bappa Rawal, revered as the “Hindua Suraj,” was among the earliest great defenders of Hindu India against the Arab-Islamic invasions of the 8th century. He united Hindu forces, defeated the advancing armies and halted their march towards India’s heartland, making Mewar a bastion of Hindu resistance. A visionary commander, he carried the fight beyond India’s frontiers, pursuing the invaders into Afghanistan and launching repeated campaigns into Ghazni and beyond, extending Mewar’s influence towards the Persian frontier. He founded Rawalpindi (now in Pakistan) as a strategic frontier garrison. His victories did more than defend Mewar—they pushed the invaders back to their own frontiers, held Islamic expansion at bay for nearly four centuries, and forged Mewar’s enduring legacy as the shield of Hindu civilisation.

Sri Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529), the greatest ruler of Vijayanagara, was a formidable defender and patron of Hindu civilisation in the Deccan. Through his military victories over the Bahmani Sultanates, he secured and expanded Vijayanagara’s power, while extensively patronising temples, religious institutions and Hindu learning. His celebrated title “Hindu Raya Suratrana”—understood as “the King who protects Hindu Dharma”—expressed his role as the sovereign protector of the Hindu religious order. Under Krishnadevaraya, Vijayanagara reached the height of its power and stood as one of the strongest political and military shields of Hindu civilisation in South India against Islamic forces.

Lachit Borphukan’s historic contribution was to halt Mughal expansion into Assam and preserve the Hindu civilisation of the Northeast. As the supreme commander of the Ahom forces under Swargadeo Chakradhwaj Singha, he recovered Guwahati from the Mughals and, at the Battle of Saraighat in 1671, decisively defeated the much larger Mughal army, frustrating Aurangzeb’s attempt to conquer Assam. His victory preserved Assam’s Hindu political sovereignty and Hindu religion from Islam. Lachit Borphukan thus stands as the warrior who stopped the Islamic advance at the Brahmaputra and made Assam the eastern bastion of Hindu resistance to Islamic expansion.

Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj (1630–1680) was the great architect of Hindu Swarajya and one of the foremost defenders of Hindu civilisation against Mughal and Deccan Sultanate domination. He united the Marathas, built a powerful and disciplined state, protected temples and religious institutions, and established a model of governance rooted in Dharma and justice for all. His military genius, fortification system and naval strength transformed resistance into a durable political power. Shivaji Maharaj’s enduring legacy is that he revived the ideal of Hindu sovereignty and demonstrated that a determined Hindu power could successfully challenge the might of the Islamic empires of his age.

Sri Birsa Munda (1875–1900), from present-day Jharkhand, was a great leader and a staunch defender of Sanatan tribal identity. He led a powerful rebellion against the Christian colonial British rule and against Christian missionaries who were engaged in converting Hindu tribal communities to Christianity. He fought to protect the Sanatan religious traditions, culture and identity of his people. It was the conspiracy of the Christian missionaries that ultimately led to his killing. For this reason, Hindus—both tribal and non-tribal—in Jharkhand and the adjoining areas of Odisha and Bengal deeply revere him and honour him as Bhagwan Birsa Munda.

Babu Jagjivan Ram (1908–1986) made a distinctive contribution to the preservation of Hindu unity by fighting for the dignity and rights of Harijans while keeping their struggle within the Hindu fold. This sharply distinguished his approach from that of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, who advocated conversion out of the Hindu fold and declared in 1935, “I will not die a Hindu,” eventually embracing Buddhism in 1956. Jagjivan Ram, by contrast, opposed religious conversion and sought to eradicate untouchability, promote temple entry, education and social equality through reform within Hindu society. His distinctive legacy was to combine social emancipation with the preservation of Hindu identity—strengthening Hindu society from within rather than allowing its most disadvantaged sections to be separated from it.
